heroText: Taipei is a Taiwan base best planned around named sights rather than a generic stopover. Start with Taipei 101, add Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, and use National Palace Museum to understand the city's history, street life and visitor rhythm. history.label: Origins
history.text: Prior to the significant influx of Han Chinese colonists, the region of Taipei Basin was mainly inhabited by the Ketagalan, a Plains Indigenous people.

history.label: 19th century
history.text: In the late 19th century, the Taipei area, where the major Han Chinese settlements in northern Taiwan and one of the designated overseas trade ports, Tamsui, were located, gained economic importance due to the.
In 1875, the northern part of the island was incorporated into the new Taipeh Prefecture.
In 1886, as work commenced to govern the island as a province, Taipeh was designated as the provincial capital.
It was formerly established as Taipeh-fu and was the temporary capital of the island in 1887 when it was declared a province (Fukien-Taiwan Province).
The romanized transcription of Taipeh was changed to Taihoku in 1895 when the Empire of Japan annexed Taiwan, based on the Japanese reading of the two characters.
During Japanese rule, Taihoku was incorporated in 1920 as part of Taihoku Prefecture.
The eastern village of Matsuyama (松山庄; modern-day Songshan District, Taipei) was annexed into Taihoku City in 1938.
After facing defeat from Communist forces, the ruling Kuomintang relocated the ROC government to Taiwan and declared Taipei the provisional capital of the ROC in December 1949.
In 1990, Taipei provided the backdrop for the Wild Lily student rallies that moved Taiwanese society from one-party rule to multi-party democracy by 1996.
